concept.name: Doji
concept.definition: A single-candlestick formation in which the open and close are equal or virtually equal, producing a very small or nonexistent real body. In technical analysis it is read as a sign of indecision between buyers and sellers; as with all candlestick patterns, it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Buyers and sellers fought to a draw during the period: price traveled up and down but ended essentially where it started, so neither side is in control.
concept.mechanics: Computed directly from OHLC data: the real body |close - open| is at or near zero relative to the period's range (a common convention classifies a candle as a doji when the body is no more than a few percent of the high-low range). The position of the open/close within the range defines subtypes (long-legged, dragonfly, gravestone).
concept.formula: Doji when |C - O| <= epsilon * (H - L), where O, H, L, C are the period's open, high, low, close and epsilon is a small threshold (often ~0.05).
concept.failure_modes: A lone doji is a neutral indicator with little information content; it appears frequently in sideways markets where it says nothing about direction. Reversal interpretations often fail without confirmation from the next candle or other indicators.
concept.misconceptions: A doji does not by itself signal a reversal; it signals indecision, and the prevailing trend can just as easily continue. It is also not rare in the absolute sense on low-liquidity or very short timeframes.
concept.example: A stock rallies for a week, then prints a daily candle that opens at 50.10 and closes at 50.12 with a high of 51.00 and low of 49.20. Analysts read the doji as waning buying momentum and wait for a bearish confirmation candle before treating it as a reversal warning.
